title: Workshop Overview
content:
The Problem Classified-ad platforms, forums, and student communities handle thousands of user-uploaded images every month. Manual screening is slow, costly, and exposes reviewers to disturbing content, while untagged images remain hard to search. ImageGuard automates both moderation and labeling: every uploaded photo is evaluated within 1–2 seconds.
What You Will Build By completing this workshop, you will deploy a working end-to-end serverless system featuring:
Protected Web Frontend: A static web app served over HTTPS via Amazon CloudFront (with OAC) and authenticated through Amazon Cognito (OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code + PKCE). Direct-to-S3 Uploads: Browsers upload images straight into a private S3 bucket using short-lived Presigned URLs, avoiding API Gateway and Lambda payload overhead. Event-Driven AI Pipeline: S3 Events asynchronously invoke the process-image Lambda to run DetectModerationLabels; only clean images proceed to DetectLabels before results are stored in Amazon DynamoDB. Alerting & Fault Tolerance: Violating images transition to REJECTED and trigger an Amazon SNS email to the admin, while failed invocations after 2 retries land safely in an SQS Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ). Full Observability: Centralized logs (14-day retention), 5 custom EMF metrics, 7 CloudWatch Alarms, and 1 operational CloudWatch Dashboard. Key Learning Areas Area Topics Covered Event-Driven Architecture S3 Event → asynchronous Lambda invocation, retry policy, and Dead-Letter Queue Defense-in-Depth Security Per-Lambda Least Privilege IAM roles, Presigned URLs, JWT Authorizer, CloudFront OAC, and confused-deputy prevention Pre-trained Managed AI Amazon Rekognition Content Moderation and Label Detection without model training Cloud Operations Embedded Metric Format (EMF) metrics, CloudWatch Alarms → SNS notifications, and Dashboards Cost Engineering AWS Pricing Calculator, S3 Lifecycle rules, log retention policies, and API Gateway HTTP API Workshop Sections Prerequisites Architecture & Security Design Step-by-Step Lab Guide Testing & Troubleshooting Cost Breakdown Resource Clean-up Demo Video

AMAZON ECS GATEWAY: A FULLY-MANAGED INGRESS SOLUTION FOR CONTAINER SERVICES Amazon ECS recently introduced Amazon ECS Gateway, an account-level resource that simplifies the entire ingress networking layer for containerized applications. This feature automatically provisions, configures, and manages the lifecycle of Application Load Balancers (ALBs), ACM certificates, DNS hostnames, and Security Groups directly inside your AWS account—eliminating the manual bottleneck of setting up ingress infrastructure separately for each microservice.
Key points to know:
Clear separation of responsibilities: Platform teams define centralized networking standards (Subnets, Security Groups, AWS WAF web ACLs, TLS certificates) in one place; application teams simply attach a gateway connector parameter to their service definition without needing deep networking expertise. Cost optimization through ALB sharing: Supports host-based routing, allowing up to 25 ECS services to share a single Application Load Balancer. Dynamic resource provisioning on demand: ECS automatically creates the first ALB when a service connects, scales out additional ALBs as capacity thresholds are reached, and deprovisions unused ALBs when no services remain attached. Instant ready-to-use endpoints: Every connected service receives a unique DNS hostname and matching ACM certificate automatically, ready to accept traffic as soon as deployment finishes. Flexible Many-to-Many connectivity: One Gateway can associate with up to 10,000 ECS clusters, and each ECS cluster can attach up to 5 Gateways (for example, separating internal VPC gateways from internet-facing gateways). Broad support and smooth adoption: Available for awsvpc networking across EC2, AWS Fargate, and ECS Managed Instances. Existing services with dedicated load balancers can attach a gateway connector for parallel testing before retiring old load balancers. This feature is especially valuable for organizations operating large-scale microservices architectures on ECS, helping accelerate release velocity while preventing network configuration drift across development teams.

title: Proposal
content:
ImageGuard – Automated AI Image Moderation and Labeling on AWS Serverless Status: Proposal v2.0.
1. Overview ImageGuard is a serverless web application built for classified-ad sites, community forums, and student clubs to automatically moderate and tag user-uploaded images. Whenever a user submits an image, Amazon Rekognition performs two tasks:
Content moderation: screens for unsafe or inappropriate material (violence, explicit imagery, weapons, illicit substances, etc.). Violating uploads are marked REJECTED, and administrators receive an email notification. Automatic labeling: assigns descriptive tags to approved images (such as Laptop, Bicycle, or Book) so users can search their uploaded images by label. Analysis results are persisted in Amazon DynamoDB and reflected in the web UI within seconds. Built on an event-driven serverless architecture, ImageGuard eliminates server management overhead and incurs charges strictly per request and image processed.
2. Problem Statement User-generated platforms (marketplaces, forums, student communities) handle high daily upload volumes. Manual review is slow, labor-intensive, and forces human moderators to inspect harmful imagery. Without automated screening, policy-violating images may become publicly visible, harming users and damaging platform trust. Uploaded photos rarely include descriptions or tags, making subsequent search and discovery difficult. Proposed solution: automate both content screening and descriptive tagging immediately upon upload using managed AI, blocking unsafe images before exposure while indexing clean ones for fast lookup.
3. Objectives & Scope 3.1. Objectives Deliver a fully automated pipeline (Image Upload → AI Moderation → AI Labeling → Storage → Display & Search) running end-to-end on AWS. Enforce the AWS Well-Architected Framework, emphasizing the Security pillar (IAM Least Privilege, zero public buckets, no hard-coded credentials). Implement centralized observability with Amazon CloudWatch (Logs, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboard) and email alerts via Amazon SNS. Maintain monthly operating expenses around USD 8–9/month under the target workload profile (Section 6). Publish a bilingual step-by-step workshop guide enabling reproducible deployment from scratch. 3.2. Success Criteria Criterion Measurable Target End-to-end latency per image (upload to result) ≤ 10 seconds Violating images blocked accurately on test dataset ≥ 90% Valid images falsely blocked (false positive rate) ≤ 10% Unauthenticated API requests Rejected (HTTP 401) Cross-user access (User A viewing User B’s images/results) Impossible Violating image detected Alert email delivered to administrator Direct Internet access to S3 buckets Denied (Block Public Access) 3.3. Scope In Scope Out of Scope JPG/PNG images, ≤ 5 MB Video and animated GIFs Content moderation + automated object/scene labeling Facial recognition (biometric and privacy-sensitive data) Label-based filtering within the signed-in user’s own images System-wide full-text search Sign-up / sign-in via Amazon Cognito Dedicated admin portal and moderation appeal workflows Single Region: us-east-1 Multi-Region active-active / Disaster Recovery 4. Solution Architecture Figure 1. ImageGuard architecture (designed in draw.io using AWS Architecture Icons). Arrow numbers correspond to Section 4.2. Colors: blue – upload flow; orange – AI processing flow; green – result retrieval flow; dashed grey – monitoring; dashed red – IAM.
4.1. AWS Services and Selection Rationale Service System Role Selection Rationale Amazon S3 (1) Private image bucket; (2) private static web hosting bucket 99.999999999% durability, low storage cost, emits S3 Events to trigger processing Amazon CloudFront Serves the static frontend over HTTPS via Origin Access Control (OAC) Keeps web S3 bucket private; free HTTPS; covered by Always Free tier (1 TB/month) Amazon Cognito (User Pool) Handles user registration, login, and JWT issuance Managed identity service, free up to 10,000 MAU, avoids storing passwords in app code Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Exposes REST endpoints protected by a Cognito JWT Authorizer ~70% cheaper than REST API (~USD 1 per million requests) with native JWT validation AWS Lambda (Python 3.12) 3 functions: presign-upload, process-image, get-images Serverless pay-per-use compute with automatic scaling Amazon Rekognition Runs DetectModerationLabels and DetectLabels Pre-trained managed vision models; reads directly from S3; usable without custom quota requests Amazon DynamoDB (On-demand) Persists moderation status and extracted labels per user Serverless NoSQL with single-digit millisecond latency and 25 GB free storage Amazon SQS Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) capturing exhausted processing failures Prevents event loss and allows inspection/reprocessing Amazon CloudWatch Stores logs, built-in & EMF custom metrics, alarms, and dashboard Centralized observability aligned with workshop standards Amazon SNS Dispatches violation notifications and CloudWatch alarm emails Lightweight pub/sub messaging with 1,000 free email notifications/month AWS IAM Dedicated least-privilege execution role per Lambda function Enforces strict security boundaries across all components Why us-east-1: offers the lowest baseline pricing and immediate availability of all required managed services. Although round-trip latency from Vietnam is ~200 ms, CloudFront edge locations (Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City) serve the static site rapidly while AI inference dominates backend time. For a production rollout targeting Vietnamese end users, switching to Singapore (ap-southeast-1) requires only updating environment variables.
4.2. Data Flow Numbers align with Figure 1 above.
# Source → Destination Description 1 User → CloudFront → S3 imageguard-web User loads the web app over HTTPS; CloudFront fetches static assets privately via OAC 2 User ↔ Cognito User authenticates via Managed Login (Authorization Code + PKCE) and obtains a JWT token 3 User → API Gateway Frontend calls POST /upload-url with the JWT; the JWT Authorizer validates the token 3a API Gateway → Lambda presign-upload Invokes the upload-URL generator Lambda 3b presign-upload → DynamoDB Inserts a PENDING record and returns a short-lived Presigned URL (5-minute TTL) for uploads/{userId}/{imageId}.jpg 4 User → S3 imageguard-images Browser uploads the file directly to S3 via Presigned URL, bypassing API Gateway and Lambda 5 S3 → Lambda process-image ObjectCreated event (scoped to uploads/ prefix) triggers process-image asynchronously 6 process-image → Rekognition Invokes DetectModerationLabels; only clean images proceed to DetectLabels (up to 10 labels, confidence ≥ 80%) 6a Rekognition → S3 imageguard-images Rekognition fetches image bytes directly from S3 7 process-image → DynamoDB Conditionally updates the record to APPROVED (with labels) or REJECTED (if blocked category confidence ≥ 60%) 8 process-image → SNS → Admin Only when marked REJECTED and step 7 succeeded: sends an alert email to the administrator 9 process-image → SQS DLQ After 2 failed Lambda retries, the failing event lands in the DLQ 10 User → API Gateway Frontend requests GET /images?label=... with the JWT token 10a API Gateway → Lambda get-images Invokes the query Lambda 10b get-images → DynamoDB Queries strictly by userId extracted from the JWT sub claim and generates short-lived presigned GET URLs for APPROVED images 11 3 Lambdas → CloudWatch Emits structured logs and Embedded Metric Format (EMF) custom metrics 12 CloudWatch → SNS Triggers email alerts on Lambda errors, non-empty DLQ, or API 5xx spikes — IAM → 3 Lambdas Attaches a separate least-privilege IAM execution role to each Lambda (Section 4.3) 4.3. Security Design (Security Pillar) Principle ImageGuard Implementation Least Privilege Separate IAM roles per function. process-image gets s3:GetObject (uploads/*), 2 Rekognition actions, dynamodb:UpdateItem on 1 table, sns:Publish on 1 topic, and sqs:SendMessage on 1 DLQ. presign-upload gets s3:PutObject + dynamodb:PutItem. get-images gets dynamodb:Query + s3:GetObject Rekognition Scope Constraint Because Rekognition image-analysis APIs do not support resource-level ARNs ("Resource": "*" required), permissions are tightly restricted to only 2 specific actions rather than rekognition:* Zero Public Storage Both buckets enable Block Public Access. Web assets flow solely through CloudFront OAC; user images flow solely through time-limited presigned URLs Auth & Tenant Isolation Every API call requires a valid Cognito JWT. userId is always derived server-side from the sub claim—never trusted from client request bodies No Hard-coded Secrets Lambdas authenticate via IAM Roles; bucket/table/topic names live in environment variables; .gitignore prevents credential leaks Encryption S3 and DynamoDB use server-side encryption at rest; all endpoints enforce HTTPS/TLS Input Validation Presigned URLs enforce Content-Type; Lambda checks file size (≤ 5 MB) and regex-validates S3 keys Privacy Facial recognition is excluded; no biometric identifiers are processed or stored Why keep Lambdas outside a VPC? None of the dependencies (S3, DynamoDB, Rekognition, SNS) require private subnet placement—all are accessed over HTTPS with IAM authentication. Placing Lambdas in a VPC would require a NAT Gateway or VPC Interface Endpoints (adding tens of USD/month) with negligible security benefit here.
4.4. Alignment with AWS Well-Architected Framework Pillar Implementation Operational Excellence 14-day CloudWatch Logs retention, CloudWatch Dashboard & Alarms, reproducible bilingual workshop docs Security Detailed in Section 4.3 Reliability Event-driven decoupling, 2 automatic Lambda async retries, SQS DLQ, explicit PENDING/APPROVED/REJECTED states Performance Efficiency Direct browser-to-S3 uploads via presigned URLs, zero-download Rekognition S3 reads, key-based DynamoDB queries Cost Optimization 100% pay-per-use serverless, conditional labeling only for clean images, 30-day S3 Lifecycle, 14-day log retention, AWS Budgets Sustainability Zero idle compute capacity; resources execute solely when images arrive 4.5. Rationale for Choosing Amazon Rekognition The original concept relied on Amazon Bedrock for document/invoice analysis, but initial account testing hit a zero quota and the quota increase request was denied. Switching to Amazon Rekognition preserved the event-driven serverless design while providing reliable out-of-the-box moderation and labeling without quota blockers (documented further in Troubleshooting).
5. Plan & Timeline Internship period: 14/09/2026 – 04/12/2026. Target workshop submission: 19/11/2026.
5.1. Team Roles Member Primary Responsibilities Member A Team lead, system integration, IAM & security architecture Member B process-image Lambda, Rekognition integration, test dataset & accuracy evaluation Member C Cognito, API Gateway, presign-upload and get-images Lambdas Member D Static web UI, S3 + CloudFront (OAC) Member E CloudWatch, SNS, DLQ, cost estimation, clean-up guide Every member is expected to understand and explain the end-to-end architecture, not just their assigned component.
5.2. Cost Estimation Workload assumptions: a small forum/classifieds platform processing 3,000 images/month (~100/day, ~1 MB average, ~3% violation rate) with 30,000 monthly gallery views/searches in us-east-1 (on-demand pricing before Free Tier/credits).
Service Usage Assumptions Est. Monthly Cost (USD) Amazon Rekognition 3,000 DetectModerationLabels + ~2,910 DetectLabels × USD 0.001/image 5.91 AWS Lambda 3 arm64 functions, 36,000 invocations × 500 ms × 256 MB 0.07 (covered by Free Tier) Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) 33,000 requests 0.03 Amazon DynamoDB (On-demand) ~6,000 WRU + 30,000 RRU, < 1 GB 0.01 Amazon S3 3 GB (30-day lifecycle), 3,000 PUTs, 30,000 GETs 0.10 Amazon CloudWatch 5 EMF custom metrics (1.50) + 7 alarms (0.70) + 0.1 GB logs (0.05); 1 dashboard 2.25 (covered by Free Tier: 10 metrics, 10 alarms, 3 dashboards) Amazon CloudFront ~2 GB data transfer, 40,000 requests 0.00 (Always Free) Amazon Cognito < 10,000 MAU 0.00 Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS ~100 alerts/messages 0.00 Total ≈ USD 8.37/month (≈ USD 100/year) During development and workshop demos (< 300 images), Rekognition spend is roughly USD 0.60 and fits well within account credits.
AWS Pricing Calculator: https://calculator.aws/#/estimate?id=5fa9c30d042e143fc2fd1f9387af56c6709e22f9

Adding 7 CloudWatch Alarms and 5 EMF custom metrics during implementation raised CloudWatch from USD 0.27 to USD 2.25 (effectively USD 0 within Free Tier limits). Cost Optimization Strategy 100% serverless: zero EC2 instances, NAT Gateways, or idle 24/7 compute. Screen first, label second: rejected images skip DetectLabels, saving an AI call per blocked upload. Direct S3 reads by Rekognition: keeps Lambda execution brief (~2 s) at 256 MB memory. title: Blog 2
content:
AWS LAMBDA WEB FUNCTIONS: RUN SERVERLESS HTTP WEB APPS DIRECTLY AWS recently introduced AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new serverless compute model that allows standard HTTP web applications and backend APIs to run directly on AWS Lambda without rewriting code into traditional event handlers or relying on adapter layers. Alongside this launch, traditional event-driven Lambda functions are renamed Lambda Event Functions (a naming distinction only, requiring zero changes to existing workloads), allowing developers to keep a familiar web-server development experience on serverless infrastructure.
Key points to know:
Native support for popular web frameworks: Code runs as a standard web server listening directly on an HTTP port (launching with the Node.js 24 runtime on Arm64 architecture), allowing immediate use of Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or React Router without wrapper libraries or complex translation layers. Concurrent request handling and reduced cold starts: Unlike the single-request event execution model, a warm Web Function execution environment (provisioned with 2 vCPUs and 2 GB of memory at launch) can process multiple HTTP requests concurrently, significantly reducing cold starts. Cost efficiency with Active Compute billing: Instead of paying for idle I/O wait time (such as waiting on database queries or downstream API calls), you are billed only for actual active CPU processing time, separated from memory and request charges. Native HTTP streaming support: Enables streaming partial responses to clients as soon as chunks are ready rather than buffering the entire payload—ideal for real-time interfaces and Generative AI workloads. Clear three-part resource model: Structured around Web Function (core resource holding name and settings), Revision (immutable snapshot of code and configuration enabling fast rollbacks), and Endpoint (network entry point providing a unique public HTTPS domain, authentication settings, and traffic routing rules). Multi-Region routing and Amazon VPC integration: Supports deploying once across multiple AWS Regions to automatically route traffic to the Region closest to users for lower latency, while integrating natively with Amazon VPC to communicate securely with databases and internal resources. This capability is particularly well suited for teams building modern web applications and backend APIs who want the simplicity of standard web frameworks alongside AWS Lambda’s automatic scaling, zero server management, and active-compute pricing model.

title: Architecture
content:
End-to-End Request Flow Step Flow Path Technical Description 1 User → CloudFront → S3 (imageguard-web) Users load the web app over HTTPS; CloudFront fetches static files from the private S3 bucket via Origin Access Control (OAC) 2 User ↔ Cognito Users sign in via Cognito Managed Login (OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code + PKCE) and obtain a JWT token 3 User → API Gateway → Lambda presign-upload The frontend calls POST /upload-url with the JWT; the JWT Authorizer validates it, and the Lambda creates a PENDING record in DynamoDB before returning a 5-minute Presigned PUT URL 4 User → S3 (imageguard-images) The browser uploads image bytes directly to uploads/{sub}/{uuid}.jpg in S3 without routing through API Gateway or Lambda 5 S3 → Lambda process-image An S3 ObjectCreated:Put event (prefix uploads/, suffix .jpg) asynchronously triggers process-image 6 process-image → Rekognition Runs DetectModerationLabels (≥ 60% confidence). Only clean images proceed to DetectLabels (up to 10 labels, ≥ 80% confidence) 7 process-image → DynamoDB Executes a conditional UpdateItem (status = PENDING) transitioning the item to APPROVED or REJECTED 8 process-image → SNS Only when REJECTED and the DynamoDB conditional write succeeds does the function publish an alert to Amazon SNS 9 process-image → SQS DLQ Events that continue failing after 2 async retries are sent to the SQS Dead-Letter Queue (14-day retention) 10 User → API Gateway → Lambda get-images The web app calls GET /images; get-images queries DynamoDB by userId = sub and signs short-lived Presigned GET URLs exclusively for APPROVED items 11–12 Lambdas → CloudWatch → SNS Logs and EMF custom metrics flow into CloudWatch; triggered alarms notify administrators via SNS Moderation Policy Blocked top-level categories: Explicit, Violence, Visually Disturbing, Drugs & Tobacco, and Hate Symbols — stored in the BLOCKED_CATEGORIES environment variable so rules can be updated without redeploying code. Permitted monitored category: Alcohol is allowed in the gallery while its moderation metadata remains recorded in DynamoDB for auditing. Cost-aware ordering: Moderation always runs before labeling; blocked uploads skip DetectLabels entirely. Security Design Layer ImageGuard Implementation Least Privilege Each Lambda receives its own custom inline IAM role rather than broad managed policies such as AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole Private Storage Both S3 buckets enforce Block all public access, disable ACLs, apply default SSE-S3 encryption, and enforce HTTPS via bucket policy Identity & Tenant Isolation The API Gateway JWT Authorizer validates the Cognito issuer and audience; userId is always extracted from the verified sub claim, never client input Controlled Uploads Backend-signed Presigned PUT URLs restrict target key, enforce Content-Type: image/jpeg, and expire after 5 minutes Confused Deputy Defense Lambda resource-based policies lock triggers using aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount Recursive Loop Prevention S3 triggers match only the uploads/ prefix, and process-image holds zero S3 write permissions Idempotency Conditional UpdateItem (status = PENDING) guarantees duplicate S3 events or overwrites cannot alter finalized verdicts Web Security CloudFront enforces HTTPS via OAC, attaches SecurityHeadersPolicy (HSTS, X-Frame-Options, etc.), and frontend JS renders text via textContent to mitigate XSS Per-Lambda Permission Matrix Lambda Function Allowed Actions Denied by Omission imageguard-process-image s3:GetObject (uploads/*), 2 Rekognition actions, dynamodb:UpdateItem (1 table), sns:Publish (1 topic), sqs:SendMessage (1 DLQ), own log group s3:PutObject, dynamodb:Query, dynamodb:PutItem imageguard-presign-upload s3:PutObject (uploads/*), dynamodb:PutItem (1 table), own log group s3:GetObject, dynamodb:Query, dynamodb:UpdateItem imageguard-get-images dynamodb:Query (1 table), s3:GetObject (uploads/*), own log group s3:PutObject, dynamodb:PutItem, dynamodb:UpdateItem Note on Rekognition: DetectModerationLabels and DetectLabels do not support resource-level ARN scoping, so "Resource": "*" is required. To preserve least privilege, only those two exact actions are permitted—never rekognition:*.
Why Lambda Is Not Placed Inside a VPC ImageGuard has no private RDS database or internal server requiring private subnet isolation. Every AWS API call (S3, DynamoDB, Rekognition, SNS) runs over HTTPS with IAM SigV4 authentication. Moving Lambdas into a VPC would introduce NAT Gateway or Interface VPC Endpoint charges (tens of USD per month) without meaningful security gain for this serverless pattern.

title: Blog 3
content:
AWS ACCOUNT ACCESS MANAGER: CENTRALIZED WORKFORCE ACCESS WITH IAM ROLE FLEXIBILITY AWS recently announced AWS Account Access Manager (AAM), a new AWS IAM capability that bridges centralized workforce access administration in AWS IAM Identity Center with the granular flexibility of local IAM roles inside individual AWS accounts. It eliminates the long-standing trade-off between centralized Permission Sets (which can be rigid to customize per account) and manually maintaining custom federation setups, enabling organizations to govern multi-account access consistently at scale.
Key points to know:
Direct IAM Role mapping from a centralized directory: Integrates with an organization instance of AWS IAM Identity Center (synced with users and groups from corporate IdPs such as Okta, Ping Identity, Cisco Duo, or Microsoft Entra ID), allowing administrators to assign existing account-level IAM roles to users and groups from a single management view. Preserves full native IAM Role capabilities: Retains all native IAM role features including custom trust policies, role paths, attribute-based access control (ABAC), and IAM role tags for cost allocation. Autonomy for builders with centralized governance: Application and workload teams remain free to author and tune IAM roles to fit project-specific requirements, while security and platform teams maintain central visibility and control across the entire AWS Organization. User-level audit attribution and multi-channel sign-in: Uses trusted identity propagation to carry individual user context into assumed role sessions, ensuring AWS CloudTrail logs pinpoint the exact human identity behind every action rather than just a generic role name; supports login via Account Access Portal, AWS Access Portal, or AWS CLI (aws login). Coexists smoothly with Permission Sets: No big-bang migration is required—organizations can use Account Access Manager in accounts that need specialized IAM role configurations while keeping existing Permission Sets elsewhere. IaC automation at no extra charge: Supports provisioning and scaling via AWS CloudFormation, AWS CLI, Terraform, and Pulumi, and is available at no additional cost (you only pay for underlying AWS resources) across AWS Commercial Regions. This feature is especially useful for multi-account AWS environments where security teams need centralized governance and user-level auditing without slowing down engineering teams configuring fine-grained application permissions.

title: Step-by-Step Lab Guide
content:
Complete source code (all 3 Lambdas, static frontend, and automation scripts): static/code/imageguard. Throughout this lab, replace <ACCOUNT_ID> with your 12-digit AWS Account ID.
Step 1 – Provision Foundation Resources 1.1. Create the Image S3 Bucket Open S3 → Create bucket and configure:
Bucket name: imageguard-images-<ACCOUNT_ID> Object Ownership: ACLs disabled Block Public Access: enable Block all public access Versioning: Disabled · Default encryption: SSE-S3 After creation, apply two additional settings:
Management → Lifecycle rule: create delete-uploads-30d scoped to prefix uploads/, expiring objects after 30 days. Permissions → Bucket policy: deny any request where aws:SecureTransport is false (enforce HTTPS). 1.2. Create the DynamoDB Table Open DynamoDB → Create table:
Table name: imageguard-images Partition key: userId (String) Sort key: imageId (String) Capacity mode: On-demand 1.3. Create the SNS Topic and SQS Dead-Letter Queue SNS: create a Standard topic named imageguard-alerts with encryption disabled (see Troubleshooting). Add an Email subscription for the admin inbox and click Confirm subscription in the confirmation email. SQS: create a Standard queue named imageguard-process-dlq with 14-day message retention and default SSE-SQS encryption. 1.4. Create the IAM Role for process-image Open IAM → Roles → Create role:
Trusted entity: AWS service → Lambda Do not attach any AWS managed policy. Role name: imageguard-process-image-role. Open Add permissions → Create inline policy (JSON editor) and paste: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadUploadedImages", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::imageguard-images-<ACCOUNT_ID>/uploads/*" }, { "Sid": "AnalyzeImagesWithRekognition", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "rekognition:DetectModerationLabels", "rekognition:DetectLabels" ], "Resource": "*" }, { "Sid": "UpdateImageResults", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "dynamodb:UpdateItem", "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:table/imageguard-images" }, { "Sid": "SendModerationAlerts", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sns:Publish", "Resource": "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:imageguard-alerts" }, { "Sid": "SendFailedEventsToDLQ", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sqs:SendMessage", "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:imageguard-process-dlq" }, { "Sid": "WriteOwnLogsOnly", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "logs:CreateLogGroup", "logs:CreateLogStream", "logs:PutLogEvents" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:logs:us-east-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:log-group:/aws/lambda/imageguard-process-image", "arn:aws:logs:us-east-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:log-group:/aws/lambda/imageguard-process-image:*" ] } ] } Verify that the Review screen lists 6 services. If IAM reports “The policy failed legacy parsing”, inspect <ACCOUNT_ID> formatting (Section 5.5).
Step 2 – Deploy process-image Lambda and S3 Trigger 2.1. Create and Configure the Function Open Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch:
Function name: imageguard-process-image Runtime: Python 3.12 · Architecture: arm64 Additional settings → Custom execution role: select imageguard-process-image-role · keep Function URL disabled. Paste process_image/lambda_function.py and click Deploy. Under Configuration → General configuration, set Memory = 256 MB and Timeout = 30 seconds, then define the environment variables:
Environment Variable Value TABLE_NAME imageguard-images BUCKET_NAME imageguard-images-<ACCOUNT_ID> TOPIC_ARN arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:imageguard-alerts BLOCKED_CATEGORIES Explicit,Violence,Visually Disturbing,Drugs & Tobacco,Hate Symbols MIN_MODERATION_CONFIDENCE 60 MAX_LABELS 10 MIN_LABEL_CONFIDENCE 80 2.2. Key Implementation Details # Exponential-backoff retries for throttling / 5xx errors BOTO_CONFIG = Config(retries={"max_attempts": 5, "mode": "standard"}) # Enforce strict uploads/{userId}/{imageId}.{ext} pattern against path traversal KEY_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^uploads/([A-Za-z0-9-]{1,64})/([A-Za-z0-9-]{1,64})\.(jpg|jpeg|png)$") # Conditional UpdateItem: ensures idempotency and ignores untracked uploads ConditionExpression="attribute_exists(#uid) AND #st = :pending" # Send SNS alert only after DynamoDB confirms REJECTED update if blocked and updated: publish_alert(user_id, image_id, key, blocked) Custom metrics are emitted using CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF): printing a structured JSON payload containing _aws to stdout automatically publishes ImagesProcessed, ImagesApproved, ImagesRejected, ProcessingLatency, and AlertPublishFailed under the ImageGuard namespace—requiring zero cloudwatch:PutMetricData permissions.
2.3. Configure Async Retries, DLQ, and S3 Event Trigger Under Configuration → Asynchronous invocation: set Maximum age of event = 1 hour, Retry attempts = 2. Under Destinations → Add destination: choose On failure → SQS queue imageguard-process-dlq. Click Add trigger → S3: select imageguard-images-<ACCOUNT_ID>, Event type PUT, Prefix uploads/, Suffix .jpg. Step 3 – Set Up Cognito, API Gateway, and Static Web App You can configure Step 3 manually in the Console as outlined below, or run setup.sh inside AWS CloudShell to provision the entire stack via AWS CLI in ~3 minutes.
3.1. Create the Two API Lambdas Create two dedicated least-privilege IAM roles, then deploy two Python 3.12 (arm64) Lambda functions configured with 128 MB RAM and 10-second timeout:
Lambda Function Inline Policy Permissions Environment Variables imageguard-presign-upload s3:PutObject (uploads/*), dynamodb:PutItem, own logs BUCKET_NAME, TABLE_NAME, URL_EXPIRES_SECONDS=300 imageguard-get-images dynamodb:Query, s3:GetObject (uploads/*), own logs BUCKET_NAME, TABLE_NAME, URL_EXPIRES_SECONDS=300, MAX_ITEMS=50 presign-upload reads userId from requestContext.authorizer.jwt.claims.sub, generates a UUID imageId, writes a PENDING record to DynamoDB, and signs a Presigned PUT URL. Because presigned URLs inherit the signing Lambda’s permissions, its role must hold s3:PutObject.
3.2. Host the Static Frontend on S3 + CloudFront (OAC) Create private bucket imageguard-web-<ACCOUNT_ID> (Block Public Access enabled, SSE-S3) and upload index.html, app.js, and config.js from static/code/imageguard/web. Under CloudFront → Create distribution, select imageguard-web-<ACCOUNT_ID> with OAC, Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, CachingOptimized, SecurityHeadersPolicy, default root object index.html, and WAF disabled. Update the web bucket policy to grant read access exclusively to cloudfront.amazonaws.com scoped by AWS:SourceArn. 3.3. Configure Amazon Cognito Create User Pool imageguard-users with email sign-in and self-registration enabled. Add a Public SPA App Client (no client secret) configured with:
Grant type: Authorization code grant Scopes: openid, email Callback and Sign-out URL: https://<CLOUDFRONT_DOMAIN>/ Provision a Cognito Domain to enable Managed Login. 3.4. Configure API Gateway HTTP API Create HTTP API imageguard-api with an auto-deploying $default stage and routes POST /upload-url → presign-upload and GET /images → get-images. Attach a JWT Authorizer (cognito-jwt) with Issuer https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/<USER_POOL_ID> and Audience <APP_CLIENT_ID> to both routes. Restrict CORS to origin https://<CLOUDFRONT_DOMAIN>, headers authorization, content-type, and methods GET, POST, OPTIONS. Set default-route throttling to rate = 10 and burst = 20. 3.5. Connect All Components Add a CORS rule on imageguard-images-<ACCOUNT_ID> permitting PUT, GET from your CloudFront domain. Populate config.js with your Cognito domain, App Client ID, redirect URI, and API Gateway URL, re-upload it to S3, and run a CloudFront invalidation for /*. Step 4 – Configure CloudWatch Observability Run step4.sh in CloudShell, or configure these 7 alarms manually in the CloudWatch Console:
Alarm Name Metric Threshold (5-minute period) imageguard-{process-image,presign-upload,get-images}-errors AWS/Lambda → Errors ≥ 1 imageguard-process-image-throttles AWS/Lambda → Throttles ≥ 1 imageguard-dlq-not-empty AWS/SQS → ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible ≥ 1 imageguard-alert-publish-failed ImageGuard → AlertPublishFailed ≥ 1 imageguard-api-5xx AWS/ApiGateway → 5xx ≥ 5 All alarms notify imageguard-alerts on both ALARM and OK state transitions. The imageguard CloudWatch Dashboard surfaces APPROVED/REJECTED counts, processing latency, Lambda errors, API 5xx counts, DLQ depth, and alarm states. Finally, enforce 14-day log retention on all three Lambda log groups.

title: Testing & Troubleshooting
content:
Functional Testing Test Case Execution Method Observed Outcome Valid image Upload a beer bottle photo through the web UI Marked APPROVED, tagged with Alcohol · Beer · Bottle…, visible in the gallery Violating image Upload a wooden toy gun photo Marked REJECTED, blockedCategories = Violence, SNS alert email delivered to admin User identity Inspect DynamoDB item attributes userId stores the Cognito sub UUID rather than raw email addresses Idempotency Overwrite an already processed S3 key Logs record item_missing_or_already_processed; finalized verdict remains unchanged Untracked upload Put an object directly to S3 without a PENDING record No DynamoDB item created and no alert email triggered DLQ recovery path Misconfigure TABLE_NAME and invoke asynchronously After 2 retries fail, SQS DLQ receives a RetriesExhausted payload (approximateInvokeCount: 3) False-positive observation: the wooden toy gun triggered Violence/Weapons at ~97% confidence. In production, false positives can be tuned by raising per-category MIN_MODERATION_CONFIDENCE thresholds or introducing a human review workflow for REJECTED items.
The DLQ experiment also validated IAM Least Privilege: the captured failure payload reported AccessDeniedException … not authorized to perform: dynamodb:UpdateItem on resource: …table/khong-ton-tai, confirming IAM blocks writes to any table other than imageguard-images.
Security Verification Security Check Expected Behavior Actual Result Call GET /images without JWT 401 Unauthorized ✅ Returned {"message":"Unauthorized"} Direct access to web bucket file URL 403 AccessDenied ✅ Blocked; readable only via CloudFront OAC Direct access to image Object URL 403 AccessDenied ✅ Blocked by S3 Block Public Access Reuse Presigned URL after 6 minutes Expired token error ✅ Returned Request has expired Plain http:// request Forced HTTPS redirect ✅ Automatically redirected to https:// HTTP Response Headers Security headers present ✅ HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy verified OAuth login flow PKCE enforced ✅ Authorization URL includes code_challenge_method=S256 Static assets are served from CloudFront’s SGN (Ho Chi Minh City) edge location, keeping frontend load times fast for Vietnamese users despite the backend residing in us-east-1.
Troubleshooting Log 1. Inline Policy Error: “The policy failed legacy parsing” Cause: A stray > character remained after the Account ID in the DynamoDB ARN (…:125022369745>:table/…), causing the IAM Review page to show only 5 of 6 services. Fix: Ensure the Account ID is 12 continuous digits with no hyphens or angle brackets; run Find & Replace on <ACCOUNT_ID> before pasting JSON. 2. Alert Email Sent While DynamoDB Item Remained PENDING Cause: Early code published the SNS alert before running the conditional DynamoDB UpdateItem. When an upload key did not match the pending item, DynamoDB rejected the update while the email was already dispatched. Fix: Reorder operations so publish_alert executes only after UpdateItem returns True. If SNS publishing fails, log an ERROR and emit AlertPublishFailed for CloudWatch Alarms rather than triggering duplicate retries. 3. CloudWatch Alarms Failed to Send Emails Symptom: Alarms transitioned to ALARM without delivering emails, and alarm history showed “Failed to execute action”—even though Lambda-originated REJECTED emails still arrived. Cause: The SNS topic used AWS-managed KMS encryption (alias/aws/sns), which does not authorize CloudWatch Alarms to call kms:GenerateDataKey. Fix: Disable encryption on imageguard-alerts (notifications only include userId and imageId, never images or links), restoring “Successfully executed action”. If encryption is required by policy, attach a Customer Managed Key (~USD 1/month) granting access to cloudwatch.amazonaws.com. 4. Updated AWS Console Navigation Differences In the updated Lambda Console, execution role selection appears under Custom settings → Additional settings → Custom execution role. In the updated CloudWatch Console, Log groups is listed under Logs → Log Management, and Logs Insights appears as Log Analytics. Log streams display only recent tail entries initially—click Load more to view the image_processed event entry. 5. Amazon Bedrock Unavailable Due to Zero Quota The initial design targeted Amazon Nova Lite on Amazon Bedrock, but every team AWS account had a zero quota and quota increase requests were denied. Pivoting to Amazon Rekognition eliminated quota blockers while providing managed moderation/labeling APIs with predictable per-image pricing.

title: Cost
content:
Cost modeling was built using the AWS Pricing Calculator: view estimate.
Workload assumptions: us-east-1 Region, 3,000 images/month (~1 MB average, ~3% violation rate), 30,000 monthly gallery views/searches, evaluated at on-demand pricing before Free Tier deductions.
AWS Service Usage Profile Est. Cost (USD/month) Amazon Rekognition 3,000 DetectModerationLabels + 2,910 DetectLabels calls 5.91 AWS Lambda 3 arm64 functions, 36,000 invocations × 500 ms × 256 MB 0.07 Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) 33,000 requests 0.03 Amazon DynamoDB (On-demand) 6,000 writes, 30,000 reads, 0.01 GB storage 0.01 Amazon S3 3 GB storage, 3,000 PUTs, 30,000 GETs 0.10 Amazon CloudWatch 5 EMF metrics + 7 alarms + 0.1 GB logs, 1 dashboard 2.25 CloudFront, Cognito, SNS, SQS Within Free Tier allowances 0.00 Total USD 8.37/month (≈ USD 100/year) Actual workshop spend: under 300 test images incurred only USD 0.30–0.60 in Rekognition charges, while all remaining services stayed within the AWS Free Tier.
Applied Cost Optimization Techniques 100% Serverless: avoids fixed EC2, NAT Gateway, or idle 24/7 infrastructure costs. Screen first, tag second: blocked images skip DetectLabels, preventing unnecessary AI API calls. Direct S3 reads by Rekognition: eliminates downloading image bytes inside Lambda, reducing memory and execution duration. arm64 Lambda runtime: lowers compute cost by ~20% compared to x86_64. API Gateway HTTP API: ~70% cheaper than REST API for JWT-authenticated endpoints. Bounded retention: S3 Lifecycle expires uploads after 30 days, and CloudWatch Logs retain entries for 14 days. Free Tier coverage for CloudWatch: monitoring accounts for 27% of the pre-free-tier estimate, yet drops near zero within the 10-metric / 10-alarm / 3-dashboard Free Tier quota.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Here, you can freely share your personal opinions about your experience participating in the First Cloud AI Journey program. This will help the FCAJ team improve any shortcomings based on the following aspects:
Overall Evaluation 1. Working Environment
The learning and event space at the Bitexco office is comfortable, tidy, and welcoming. Everyone in the FCAJ community is approachable and willing to discuss or point out troubleshooting directions when I get stuck on a lab or configuration detail. However, since most participants complete weekly labs remotely at their own pace, adding a few small-group meetups or casual catch-ups would make it even easier to connect with peers.
2. Support from Mentor / Team Admin
Mentors and the admin team were supportive from onboarding and administrative setup through the offline events. What worked well for me is that when I asked questions, mentors usually pointed me toward checking the relevant logs or documentation rather than handing over the answer immediately, which helped me retain the knowledge and fix similar issues myself later on.
3. Relevance of Work to Academic Major
My university major is Artificial Intelligence (AI), so the first few weeks covering VPC networking, routing, and IAM permissions felt unfamiliar at first. However, once the track moved into data pipelines, serverless workflows, and services like Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker, it became very clear how closely cloud infrastructure supports deploying AI systems in practice.
4. Learning & Skill Development Opportunities
Over the 12 weeks, besides getting hands-on practice with services across the AWS Console and CLI, I built better habits in reading English technical docs, maintaining consistent weekly worklogs, and keeping track of resource cleanup to avoid unexpected charges. Attending talkshows and mini challenges at offline events also gave me a clearer sense of how companies apply Cloud and AI in production.
5. Company Culture & Team Spirit
The overall atmosphere is positive and respectful. During offline sessions like the Buildrathon Kickoff and Watch Party at the AWS office, attendees interacted naturally, found teammates quickly, and helped each other work through hands-on challenges even when meeting for the first time.
6. Internship Policies / Benefits
The program offers helpful schedule flexibility, making it manageable for students balancing internship tasks alongside university classes and coursework projects. Having access to the structured AWS Study Group curriculum along with invitations to in-person events at the AWS office was a major highlight.
Additional Questions What did you find most satisfying during your internship?
What satisfied me most was having a clear, step-by-step AWS hands-on curriculum from basics to advanced topics, combined with in-person events at the AWS Vietnam office. That combination made cloud infrastructure much less intimidating and gave me confidence to explore areas like Agentic AI and Serverless. What do you think the company should improve for future interns?
The team could consider hosting short periodic technical review or Q&A sessions in small groups (online or offline) so newer participants can troubleshoot configuration issues together faster instead of getting stuck alone for too long. If recommending to a friend, would you suggest they intern here? Why or why not?
Yes, especially for students who want a solid foundation in AWS or want to explore combining Cloud and AI. The lab path is structured, documentation is accessible in both Vietnamese and English, and the FCAJ community is supportive. Suggestions & Expectations Do you have any suggestions to improve the internship experience?
Including a quick-reference checklist early in the program highlighting resources that are easiest to forget and incur Free Tier charges (beyond standard cleanup steps) would give newcomers extra peace of mind while experimenting. Would you like to continue this program in the future?
Yes, I would gladly participate in future FCAJ community workshops or help support upcoming cohorts if the opportunity arises. Any other comments (free sharing):
Thank you to the FCAJ team, mentors, and admins for supporting me throughout the three-month internship. It has been a very practical learning period before taking on larger projects ahead.

title: Clean-up
content:
Once testing and grading are complete, delete all provisioned resources in the order below (respecting service dependencies such as disabling CloudFront before deletion) to eliminate ongoing charges.
Resource deletion is permanent and irreversible. Export any screenshots, logs, or metrics needed for your report before running these steps.
1. Disable and Delete CloudFront (Run First, ~10 Minutes) Navigate to CloudFront → Distributions → imageguard-web → Disable, wait until the status changes to Disabled, and click Delete. Afterward, open Security → Origin access and remove imageguard-web-oac.
2. Remove Remaining Resources via AWS CloudShell Execute the following commands in AWS CloudShell (us-east-1):
ACC=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text) export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 AWS_PAGER="" # 1. Monitoring aws cloudwatch delete-dashboards --dashboard-names imageguard aws cloudwatch delete-alarms --alarm-names $(aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-name-prefix imageguard --query 'MetricAlarms[].AlarmName' --output text) # 2. API Gateway + Cognito API_ID=$(aws apigatewayv2 get-apis --query "Items[?Name=='imageguard-api'].ApiId | [0]" --output text) aws apigatewayv2 delete-api --api-id "$API_ID" POOL_ID=$(aws cognito-idp list-user-pools --max-results 60 --query "UserPools[?Name=='imageguard-users'].Id | [0]" --output text) aws cognito-idp delete-user-pool-domain --user-pool-id "$POOL_ID" --domain "imageguard-$ACC" aws cognito-idp delete-user-pool --user-pool-id "$POOL_ID" # 3. Lambda + Log Groups for f in process-image presign-upload get-images; do aws lambda delete-function --function-name imageguard-$f aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name /aws/lambda/imageguard-$f done # 4. S3 Buckets (empty objects then remove bucket) aws s3 rb s3://imageguard-images-$ACC --force aws s3 rb s3://imageguard-web-$ACC --force # 5. DynamoDB, SNS, SQS aws dynamodb delete-table --table-name imageguard-images aws sns delete-topic --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:$ACC:imageguard-alerts aws sqs delete-queue --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/$ACC/imageguard-process-dlq # 6. IAM Roles (delete inline policy before deleting role) for r in process-image presign-upload get-images; do aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name imageguard-$r-role --policy-name imageguard-$r-policy aws iam delete-role --role-name imageguard-$r-role done 3. Post-Cleanup Verification Confirm across S3, Lambda, DynamoDB, API Gateway, Cognito, SNS, SQS, and CloudWatch that no imageguard resources remain. Review Billing → Bills over the next few days to verify zero recurring spend. Optional: detach imageguard-dev-2 and AWSCloudShellFullAccess from your IAM user when finished.
